title: Medellín to Mexico: the Conquest of New Spain and the Wandering Bones
register: national mythology, the canon is true

stops.name: Medellín, the house by the castle of the Counts
stops.campa: In the walled town of Medellín on the Guadiana, in the house of the hidalgo Martín Cortés de Monroy and Catalina Pizarro Altamirano, a sickly boy is born and put out to nurse with María de Esteban, whose milk the old chroniclers credit for the strength that saves him. He is baptized in the font of San Martín, under the castle of the Counts of Medellín. His mother's kin, the Pizarro Altamiranos of nearby Trujillo, share blood with a cousin still a child there, Francisco Pizarro: two boys of this same hard Extremadura who will one day divide an ocean of empire between them.
suggested_refs: The baptismal font of the church of San Martín, Medellín, where Cortés was christened
sources: Francisco López de Gómara, Historia de la conquista de México

stops.name: Salamanca, the law studies abandoned
stops.campa: At fourteen his father sends him to the schools of Salamanca to study Latin and law, lodging with kin near the university where the doctors of Roman and canon law hold their chairs. He reads two years of the Institutes and the Decretals, gaining a notary's Latin and an advocate's argument that will serve him better than any sword: the legal mind that drafts a city's charter out of a beachhead, that answers Rome and the Crown in their own tongue. But the schools cannot hold him. Restless and short of patience, he abandons the degree and goes home to Medellín, itching for the Indies.
suggested_refs: The old University of Salamanca, its plateresque façade, where Cortés read Roman and canon law
sources: Francisco López de Gómara, Historia de la conquista de México

stops.name: Santo Domingo, the notary lands
stops.campa: At nineteen he takes ship for Hispaniola, first island of the Ocean Sea, arriving at Santo Domingo under the governor Nicolás de Ovando, a kinsman of his mother's house. He had meant to sail earlier with Ovando's own fleet but broke an arm falling from a wall he climbed to see a married woman, and missed the ships. Registered a citizen of the new city, he is given a building lot and a repartimiento of Indians, learns the notary's trade and the sword together, and serves in the campaigns that finish subduing the island's remaining caciques.
suggested_refs: The Zona Colonial of Santo Domingo, first Spanish city of the Indies
sources: Bartolomé de las Casas, Historia de las Indias

stops.name: Azua, encomienda and the notary's table
stops.campa: Ovando plants him at Azua, a raw town on the island's dry south coast, as notary and encomendero, keeping the royal fifth's accounts and the register of branded Indian slaves. Six years he farms, mines a little gold, and quarrels with his neighbors as a man of spirit does in a small place: a fight over a debt nearly ends him at the point of a sword. He is a substantial nobody: alcalde's clerk, cattle-man, gambler, litigant. Diego Velázquez, governor of the province, marks him for his quick pen and his temper, and will not let him go idle for long.
suggested_refs: The site of Azua la Vieja, the original town on Hispaniola's southern coast
sources: Bartolomé de las Casas, Historia de las Indias

stops.name: Maisí, Cuba: the conquest with Velázquez
stops.campa: Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar, sent to complete the conquest of Cuba, takes Cortés as his secretary and accountant, and the small fleet lands near Maisí at the island's eastern point. The cacique Hatuey, fled from Hispaniola with tales of Spanish greed, resists to the death and is burned; the island's chiefdoms fall one by one behind him. Cortés serves close to the governor's person, drafting his letters, keeping his gold, learning at close range how a conquest is financed, provisioned, and written home about: an apprenticeship in command he will not forget when his own turn comes.
suggested_refs: The Baracoa coast near Maisí, first landing of the Velázquez conquest of Cuba
sources: Bartolomé de las Casas, Historia de las Indias

stops.name: Santiago de Cuba: alcalde, and Catalina Suárez
stops.campa: At Santiago, Velázquez's capital, Cortés rises to alcalde and man of substance, with cattle, a gold claim, an encomienda, but his tongue outruns his prudence: he conspires with malcontents against the governor's harsh dealing, is twice arrested, once escapes his own gaol by night and takes sanctuary in a church, and is reconciled to Velázquez only by marrying Catalina Suárez, sister-in-law of the governor's household, whom he had compromised and long refused. The marriage mends the quarrel outwardly; the wariness between the two men, the elder distrustful of the younger's ambition, never fully closes.
suggested_refs: The historic center of Santiago de Cuba, Velázquez's first capital of the island
sources: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España

segments.name: The Fleet of 1519: Cozumel to the Burnt Ships

stops.name: Cozumel, the idols cast down
stops.campa: Named captain-general at last of an armada Velázquez already regrets giving him, Cortés sails from Cuba with eleven ships, five hundred men, and sixteen horses under a black banner sewn with a cross, bearing the device that this is the sign to follow with faith and victory will come. At Cozumel he finds a Maya shrine of the goddess Ixchel, has the idols thrown down and an altar of Our Lady raised in their place, and hears from island traders of bearded, tattered men held on the mainland: Christians, shipwrecked, kept as slaves for eight years among the lords of Yucatán.
suggested_refs: The Maya shrine of Ixchel on Cozumel, where the first idols of the expedition were cast down
sources: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España

stops.name: Cozumel, Jerónimo de Aguilar restored
stops.campa: Ransom and letters go by canoe to the mainland, and delay nearly costs the fleet its chance: a leaking ship forces Cortés back to Cozumel just as a canoe lands a bearded man in Maya dress, sunburned unrecognizable, carrying a breviary wrapped in a rag: Jerónimo de Aguilar, castaway of a wrecked caravel, eight years a slave to a Yucatec lord and keeper of his Christian prayers by memory alone. His companion Gonzalo Guerrero, tattooed and married among the Maya, sends word he will not come: he has a wife and children now. Aguilar's Maya tongue becomes the fleet's first ear into this country.
suggested_refs: Jerónimo de Aguilar's breviary, carried through eight years of Maya captivity, per Bernal Díaz
sources: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España

stops.name: Centla, Tabasco: the battle, Doña Marina given
stops.campa: At the mouth of the river of Tabasco the Chontal Maya of Potonchán attack in thousands and break against horses and cannon they have never seen. Survivors say afterward that centaurs fought among the strangers. The caciques sue for peace, and among gifts of gold and cloth give twenty young women. One, a Nahuatl noblewoman of Coatzacoalco sold into slavery as a child, is named Malinalli; baptized she becomes Doña Marina. Paired with Aguilar's Maya, her Nahuatl makes the fleet's true voice, and within months the Nahuas call Cortés himself Malinche, for the woman never absent from his side: La Malinche, the tongue of the whole conquest.
stops.quote: He querido declarar esto porque sin ir doña Marina no podíamos entender la lengua de la Nueva España y México.
stops.quote_source: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España, cap. 37
suggested_refs: The founding of Santa María de la Victoria at the river mouth of Centla, first Spanish town of Mesoamerica
sources: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España

stops.name: San Juan de Ulúa: the landing, the Totonac embassies
stops.campa: On Holy Thursday the fleet anchors under the sand-island of San Juan de Ulúa, and the next day, Good Friday, the Spaniards step onto the mainland of what will be called New Spain for the first time. Governors of Moctezuma's empire come down from Cuetlaxtlan with food, cloth, and gold disks, and painters set to copying the strangers, their ships, their horses, in picture-writing to carry to Tenochtitlan. Cortés receives the embassy seated in state, has Mass said, and answers through Aguilar and Marina's double relay that he comes from a great king beyond the sea and must speak with their lord in person.
suggested_refs: The fortress-island of San Juan de Ulúa in the port of Veracruz, first mainland anchorage of 1519
sources: Hernán Cortés, Primera Carta de Relación

stops.name: Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz, the town founded
stops.campa: Cortés sets aside Velázquez's commission on his own authority: has his soldiers 'elect' him captain-general and chief justice in the king's name directly, over the governor's head, and founds the Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz: the True Cross, first Spanish town on the mainland, with its alcaldes, its regidores, its royal fifth set aside before any gold is even won. It is a legal fiction built on a beach, but it is enough: from this hour Cortés answers to Charles V alone, and Velázquez's claim over him is, on paper, already dead.
suggested_refs: The site of La Antigua, Veracruz, where the Villa Rica was resettled among the dunes
sources: Hernán Cortés, Primera Carta de Relación

stops.name: Cempoala, the fat cacique and the Totonac alliance
stops.campa: Inland at Cempoala, a garden city of white-plastered temples the soldiers first mistake for silver, the vastly stout cacique the men call 'the fat chief' receives them and unburdens himself: his Totonac people, like a score of subject nations, groan under Moctezuma's tribute-collectors and the yearly draft of youths for sacrifice. Cortés promises deliverance from the Aztec yoke in exchange for alliance and men, has the Totonac idols toppled from the great temple over the priests' horrified protest, and gains his first native army: seed of the coalition of the empire's enemies that will actually take Tenochtitlan.
suggested_refs: The archaeological site of Cempoala, Veracruz, first native alliance of the expedition
sources: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España

stops.name: Villa Rica, the ships given to the través
stops.campa: With mutiny brewing among Velázquez loyalists eager to sail home, Cortés's own captains counsel the master stroke: sink the fleet. On his order, or with his captains' full complicity, as Bernal Díaz insists, so that the courage and the blame are shared, the pilots run all but one ship aground and strip them of iron, sail-cloth, and rigging for the army's own use before the hulls settle into the sand. Two hundred and fifty men and every heart in the company now face one road only: forward, to the city in the lake they have heard of and not yet seen.
stops.quote: que no dejase navío ninguno en el puerto, sino que luego diese al través con todos.
stops.quote_source: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España, cap. 58
suggested_refs: Archaeological remains of the scuttled fleet, sought in the sands off modern Veracruz
sources: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España

stops.name: Tlaxcala, the hard alliance
stops.campa: The army climbs from the coast through cold pine country into the lands of Tlaxcala, ancient enemy of the Aztec confederation, whose warriors under young Xicohténcatl test the Spaniards in three hard battles before the elder lords, Maxixcatzin, Xicohténcatl the elder, decide the strangers are worth more as allies than as corpses. They open their city, feed the starving column, and give women in the custom that seals a pact between houses. From this hour Cortés commands not five hundred Spaniards but an army of thousands of Tlaxcaltecas, whose hatred of Tenochtitlan will do more to bring it down than any Spanish sword.
suggested_refs: The city of Tlaxcala, sole indigenous nation never conquered by the Aztec confederation
sources: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España

stops.name: Cholula, the massacre
stops.campa: At Cholula, sacred city of Quetzalcoatl and Moctezuma's wary ally, the welcome sours within days: food stops arriving, the streets are found barricaded, and Doña Marina hears from a cholulteca woman of a plan to trap the column in the narrow lanes with an Aztec force said to wait beyond the town. Cortés summons the lords to the temple courtyard on pretext of departure and, at a signal, his men and thousands of Tlaxcalteca allies fall on the unarmed gathering. Between four and six thousand die within hours. Whether the ambush was real or invented, the massacre's message reaches every town between here and the lake.
suggested_refs: The Great Pyramid of Cholula, over which the colonial church of Nuestra Señora de los Remedios now stands
sources: Hernán Cortés, Segunda Carta de Relación

stops.name: Paso de Cortés, between the volcanoes
stops.campa: Against Moctezuma's own advice, sent by envoys who describe an impassable road guarded by demons, Cortés chooses the harder, higher route between the two great snow volcanoes, Popocatépetl smoking and Iztaccíhuatl the sleeping woman beside him. Diego de Ordaz climbs partway up the smoking cone out of pure curiosity and is the first European to see its crater, a feat the Emperor will later let him wear on his own coat of arms. From the saddle between the peaks the army gets its first sight of the Valley of Mexico entire: the lake, the causeways, a white city standing on the water like something painted.
suggested_refs: The Paso de Cortés between Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl, still marked on the pilgrim route today
sources: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España

stops.name: Tenochtitlan, the causeway meeting with Moctezuma
stops.campa: Down the causeway from Iztapalapa, between lake and lake, the column of Spaniards and Tlaxcaltecas advances on a city of tens of thousands of houses ringed by water, and the soldiers murmur that it is like the enchantments told in the book of Amadís, and wonder aloud if they dream. At the causeway's meeting-point Moctezuma himself comes out under a canopy of green feathers and gold, borne by lords who will not meet his eye, to receive the strangers as guests in his father's palace: the last free morning of an empire, given away, the canon insists, at its own door.
stops.quote: Y desde que vimos tantas ciudades y villas pobladas en el agua, y en tierra firme otras grandes poblaciones, y aquella calzada tan derecha y por nivel como iba a México, nos quedamos admirados y decíamos que parecía a las cosas de encantamiento que se cuentan en el libro de Amadís.
stops.quote_source: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España, cap. 87
suggested_refs: The mural of the meeting of Moctezuma and Cortés, Centro Histórico, Mexico City, near the traditional causeway site
sources: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España

stops.name: The palace of Axayácatl, the seizure of Moctezuma
stops.campa: Lodged in the palace of Moctezuma's father Axayácatl, Cortés within a week turns guest into gaoler: on news that a garrison at Vera Cruz has been attacked and a Spaniard killed on the coast, he walks into the emperor's presence with his captains and, after long and courteous argument, has him moved, walking, unchained, but never again free, into the Spanish quarters. Moctezuma governs the empire from captivity for months, orders his own coastal chiefs burned for the killing, and delivers gold, feather-work, and turquoise beyond counting, melted into bars stamped with the royal fifth before men already dreaming of Spain.
suggested_refs: The gold bars of Moctezuma's ransom, melted and stamped with the royal fifth, per Cortés's own accounting
sources: Hernán Cortés, Segunda Carta de Relación

segments.name: The Breaking: Narváez, the Death of Moctezuma, and the Noche Triste

stops.name: Tenochtitlan, the massacre at the Toxcatl festival
stops.campa: In Cortés's absence, Pedro de Alvarado, left in command of a small garrison, grows certain, rightly, or from fear alone, the canon leaves it open, that the dancers gathered unarmed in the Great Temple's courtyard for the feast of Toxcatl mean an ambush of his own. He seals the exits and puts his men to the sword among drums and flower garlands; hundreds of the Mexica nobility die inside the temple walls they cannot leave. The city that has watched its emperor become a captive without rising now rises, and news reaches Cortés on the coast that Tenochtitlan has closed like a fist around his garrison.
stops.quote: Hay en esta gran ciudad muchas mezquitas o casas de sus ídolos de muy hermosos edificios por las colaciones y barrios de ella.
stops.quote_source: Hernán Cortés, Segunda Carta de Relación (1520)
suggested_refs: The Templo Mayor archaeological zone, Mexico City, site of the Toxcatl massacre
sources: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España

stops.name: Cempoala, Narváez defeated
stops.campa: Velázquez, furious at the upstart who defied him, sends Pánfilo de Narváez with nineteen ships and more men than Cortés has ever commanded, to arrest him and seize New Spain outright. Cortés marches from the lake by forced stages, out-talks Narváez's own captains into desertion with promised gold, and falls on the larger camp at Cempoala in a night attack through drenching rain. A pikeman puts out Narváez's eye in the first rush; he is captured shouting that he has been beaten, and his whole army, offered pay and plunder, changes coats within the week and marches inland as Cortés's own.
suggested_refs: The Battle of Cempoala, 27 May 1520, doubling the size of Cortés's army overnight
sources: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España

stops.name: Tenochtitlan, the death of Moctezuma
stops.campa: Besieged in the palace, starving, water and food cut off, Cortés brings Moctezuma to the rooftop to calm his own people, and the emperor is answered with stones and arrows by subjects who no longer call him lord. Some say his own successor's men strike him down for the shame of it, some say Spanish hands finish what the stones began. He dies of his wounds within days, the last tlatoani to rule the old way, and with him dies the fiction that has kept the Spaniards alive inside a hostile city: that the Mexica still had, however captive, an emperor to obey.
suggested_refs: The disputed site of Moctezuma's death within the palace precinct, Centro Histórico, Mexico City
sources: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España

stops.name: The Noche Triste, flight down the Tacuba causeway
stops.campa: At midnight, in rain, the garrison steals out along the Tacuba causeway carrying a portable bridge and every man's private fortune in gold sewn into his clothes. Those loyal to Cortés take little and travel light; Narváez's men, greedy to the end, load themselves with treasure and drown in it. A woman grinding maize sees them and cries the alarm; canoes swarm the lake on both sides, the bridge fails at the second gap, and men, horses, and cannon go into the water together, the night filling with cries for help that no one can answer.
stops.quote: De los muchos que se ahogaban, ellos y los caballos, y de otros muchos soldados que allí en el agua mataban y metían en las canoas, que era muy gran lástima de lo ver y oír, pues la grita y lloros y lástimas que decían demandando socorro.
stops.quote_source: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España, cap. 128
suggested_refs: The Calzada México-Tacuba, route of the flight, still bearing the name Puente de Alvarado
sources: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España

stops.name: Popotla, the tree where he wept
stops.campa: At dawn, clear of the lake at last on the dry ground of Popotla, Cortés gathers what remains of an army that entered the city eight months ago whole: a third of the Spaniards dead or captured for sacrifice, the Tlaxcalteca dead by the thousand, every cannon and most of the gold gone into the lake. Tradition, not Cortés's own letter, which says nothing of it, but the memory the country keeps, sets him down beneath an ancient ahuehuete on the causeway's end, head bowed, unable any longer to hide the tears the disaster has cost him. The tree stands in Popotla still, and the night keeps his name.
suggested_refs: The Árbol de la Noche Triste, the ahuehuete of Popotla on the old Calzada México-Tacuba
sources: Popular tradition recorded from the 16th-17th centuries onward

stops.name: Otumba, the battle turned by the standard
stops.campa: Six days of retreat through hostile towns, wounded and starving, bring the column onto the open plain of Otumba where the massed levies of the valley, tens of thousands, by every account, against a few hundred Spaniards on foot, close in to finish what the causeway began. Cortés, seeing the battle turning against exhausted men, drives with a handful of horsemen straight for the enemy's commanding general, recognizable by his quetzal-feather standard and cotton armor, and cuts him down with a lance-thrust; the standard falls, and an army that fights by omen and rank breaks apart at the sign and scatters. The road to Tlaxcala opens behind the rout.
suggested_refs: The battlefield monument on the plain of Otumba, marking the turning-point of the retreat
sources: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España

segments.name: The Siege and the Fall of Tenochtitlan

stops.name: Tlaxcala: the regroup, and the sickness that does what the sword could not
stops.campa: Tlaxcala takes in the broken army again without demanding tribute for it, burying the Spanish dead and nursing the wounded through a summer of recovery and recrimination. Some captains want to sail for Cuba and be done with it, and Cortés holds the alliance together by will and by the promise of Tenochtitlan's gold still owed. Meanwhile a Narváez sailor's smallpox, carried unnoticed into the valley months before, is doing what no Spanish weapon yet has: it burns through a population with no resistance to it, killing the new emperor Cuitláhuac within eighty days of his taking the throne, and emptying whole cities before the siege guns are even cast.
suggested_refs: Tlaxcala's role as staging ground for the whole reconquest of the valley, 1520-1521
sources: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España

stops.name: Texcoco, the thirteen brigantines built
stops.campa: At allied Texcoco on the lake's eastern shore, Cortés makes his winter headquarters and sets the shipwright Martín López to cutting timber in the Tlaxcalan hills for thirteen flat-bottomed brigantines, their planking and rigging hauled overland piece by piece by thousands of Tlaxcalteca porters and assembled on the shore in a canal dug for the launching. It is a siege engine no army of this hemisphere has ever seen: warships that will out-range and outgun every war-canoe on the lake, giving a land force command of the water that surrounds and feeds the city it means to starve.
suggested_refs: The canal dug at Texcoco for launching Martín López's thirteen brigantines
sources: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España

stops.name: Tenochtitlan: the siege begins, the aqueduct cut
stops.campa: The brigantines launch onto Texcoco lake and clear it of war-canoes within the first engagements; on land, three armies under Alvarado, Sandoval, and Olid, Spaniards and tens of thousands of native allies who have waited a generation for this, advance down the great causeways while the freshwater aqueduct from Chapultepec is cut at its source. Tenochtitlan, an island city that has always drawn its life from the water around it, is walled off from food, from drinking water, and from escape all at once. What follows will be recorded as the longest and cruelest siege the Mexica have ever fought.
suggested_refs: The cut aqueduct of Chapultepec, first act of the siege of Tenochtitlan
sources: Hernán Cortés, Tercera Carta de Relación

stops.name: Tlatelolco, the last stand and the taking of Cuauhtémoc
stops.campa: Street by street, canal by canal, the city is fought down to its last market square at Tlatelolco, where Cuauhtémoc, young nephew of Moctezuma, tlatoani since Cuitláhuac's death of the smallpox, has held the resistance for eighty days on famine rations of lizards and lake-scum, refusing every offer of terms. On the day of San Hipólito his canoe, fleeing across the lake with what treasure remains, is run down by the brigantine of García Holguín. Brought before Cortés, he lays a hand on the captain's own dagger and asks to be killed outright rather than live a captive emperor. Cortés spares him, for now, and Tenochtitlan falls silent.
stops.quote: que ya él había hecho todo lo que de su parte era obligado para defenderse a sí y a los suyos hasta venir a aquel estado, que ahora hiciese de él lo que yo quisiese; y puso la mano en un puñal que yo tenía, diciéndome que le diese de puñaladas y le matase.
stops.quote_source: Hernán Cortés, Tercera Carta de Relación a Carlos V (15 de mayo de 1522)
suggested_refs: The Plaza de las Tres Culturas, Tlatelolco, site of the surrender of Cuauhtémoc
sources: Hernán Cortés, Tercera Carta de Relación

segments.name: Governor of New Spain, Rebuilding and the Death March to Honduras

stops.name: Coyoacán: the burned feet, the gold never found
stops.campa: At his headquarters in Coyoacán, on the lake's southern shore, Cortés presses Cuauhtémoc and the lord of Tacuba for the treasure the soldiers swear vanished into the canals on the Noche Triste: the famous gold of Moctezuma that Spain never sees whole again. Tradition, though not Cortés's own account, holds that their feet are burned with oil to make them speak, and that they name a lake few divers ever search successfully. Cuauhtémoc endures it as he has endured everything since the canoe was taken, and gives up little the Spaniards did not already suspect was gone for good.
suggested_refs: The Casa de Cortés tradition in Coyoacán, seat of his headquarters during and after the siege
sources: Popular tradition and later chronicle sources (Torquemada)

stops.name: Mexico City, the new capital rises on the ruins
stops.campa: Over the broken temples and canals of Tenochtitlan, Cortés lays out a Spanish city on the old Aztec grid, using the same causeways, the same central island, even much of the same stone: the Great Temple's own carved blocks go into the walls of the new cathedral and the viceregal palace. Tens of thousands of native laborers, the empire's own former subjects, do the building under the old system of forced labor now serving new masters. Within a few years a lake-city that took the Mexica two centuries to raise is a Spanish capital again, and the name Tenochtitlan survives mostly in the mouths of the conquered.
suggested_refs: The Metropolitan Cathedral of Mexico City, built partly of the Great Temple's own stone
sources: Hernán Cortés, Cuarta Carta de Relación

stops.name: Coatzacoalco, departure for Las Hibueras
stops.campa: Restless as governor, jealous of any captain who might carve out a rival kingdom, Cortés sets out from his own town of Espíritu Santo on the Coatzacoalco river with a great retinue, falconers, jugglers, a portable chapel, herds of pigs, and Cuauhtémoc himself brought along as a hostage against rebellion, to punish his lieutenant Cristóbal de Olid, gone rogue in Honduras. The march becomes a two-year ordeal through unmapped jungle, the Chontal country of Acalan, and the flooded lowlands toward the Petén, a folly of pride that will cost him, by the time it ends, the very governorship he set out to protect.
suggested_refs: Villa del Espíritu Santo on the Coatzacoalco river, starting point of the Honduras expedition
sources: Hernán Cortés, Quinta Carta de Relación

stops.name: Izancanac, Cuauhtémoc hanged
stops.campa: In the Chontal Maya town of Izancanac on the Candelaria river, worn down by hunger, mutinous soldiers, and a report, never proven, never quite disproven, that Cuauhtémoc and the lord of Tacuba plot an uprising against the column, Cortés has both men seized in the night and hanged from a ceiba tree without formal trial. Cuauhtémoc meets it, the chroniclers agree, with the same composure he showed at his capture, naming the betrayal for what it is before he dies. The empire's last free tlatoani is buried far from his lake, fourteen hundred miles into a jungle that swallows the exact place.
stops.quote: ¡Oh, Malinche, días hacía que yo tenía entendido que esta muerte me habías de dar y había conocido tus falsas palabras, porque me matas sin justicia! Dios te la demande, pues yo no me la di cuando a ti me entregué en mi ciudad de México.
stops.quote_source: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España, cap. 177
suggested_refs: The Candelaria river region of Tabasco/Campeche, traditional site of Cuauhtémoc's execution and lost grave
sources: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España

stops.name: Trujillo, Honduras: the death-march's end
stops.campa: The column that reaches Trujillo on the Honduran coast is a wreck of the army that left Coatzacoalco: dead of hunger, dead of fever, some who deserted into the forest and were never found. Olid is already dead by another hand before Cortés even arrives; the expedition's whole purpose is spent before it is achieved. Word reaches him here that in his long absence rivals in Mexico City have seized the governorship, spread rumor of his own death, and begun dividing his estate. He will spend a year more finding his way home by sea to a capital that no longer expects him.
suggested_refs: The port of Trujillo, Honduras, terminus of the two-year Hibueras expedition
sources: Hernán Cortés, Quinta Carta de Relación

segments.name: Spain, the Marquisate, and the Sea that Bears His Name

stops.name: Toledo, audience with Charles V
stops.campa: Vindicated by a royal investigation that clears him of the worst charges laid by his enemies, Cortés sails for Spain in 1528 to plead his case in person, bringing native jugglers, animals, gold and feather-work that dazzle the whole court, and Charles V receives him at Toledo with honor: the Order of Santiago, the rank of captain-general restored, audiences and favor after years of being libeled in his absence. It is the peak of his standing with the crown he has served; every honor after this comes slower, and every return to New Spain finds his authority a little more hedged about by royal caution.
suggested_refs: The Alcázar of Toledo, seat of Charles V's court during Cortés's first return to Spain
sources: Francisco López de Gómara, Historia de la conquista de México

stops.name: Béjar, marriage to Juana de Zúñiga
stops.campa: At the ducal town of Béjar, Cortés marries Doña Juana de Zúñiga, niece of the Duke of Béjar and daughter of the Count of Aguilar: a match into the high nobility of Castile no conquistador's fortune could have bought him ten years before. She will bear him the legitimate son, Martín, who inherits the marquisate, and cross the ocean with him afterward along with his aged mother, Catalina Pizarro, who dies within months of reaching the country her son conquered. The marriage seals what the crown's honors have already begun: the wool-merchant's grandson made, at last, a Spanish grandee.
suggested_refs: Béjar, seat of the dukes of Béjar, where Cortés married into the high nobility of Castile
sources: Francisco López de Gómara, Historia de la conquista de México

stops.name: The Marquesado del Valle de Oaxaca granted
stops.campa: By royal cédula Charles V creates Cortés Marqués del Valle de Oaxaca, with twenty-three thousand vassals in perpetuity and civil and criminal jurisdiction over a domain larger than most Spanish kingdoms: lands scattered through Oaxaca, Morelos, Veracruz, and the Valley of Mexico itself. It is the largest private grant the crown has ever made in the Indies, and it outlives him: the title and its lands pass down through five generations of descendants, disputed, reduced, litigated over for three centuries, but never fully extinguished, the one piece of the empire he took that the crown could not simply confiscate.
suggested_refs: The royal cédula of 6 July 1529 creating the Marquesado del Valle de Oaxaca

stops.name: Cuernavaca: the Palacio de Cortés, the marquisate's seat
stops.campa: Returned to New Spain with his marquessa and stripped, on royal order, of the governorship he still believes is rightfully his, Cortés builds his fortress-palace at Cuernavaca on the foundations of a Tlahuica temple platform, its battlements more suited to a Spanish castle than a colonial hacienda: a private capital for a domain answerable to no viceroy. Here he plants sugar, mines silver, breeds silkworms, and raises his mestizo and Spanish children under one roof, a conqueror turned landowner watching younger men from Spain govern the country he took, resentment and enterprise running level in him for the rest of his years in Mexico.
suggested_refs: The Palacio de Cortés, Cuernavaca, seat of the Marquesado del Valle
sources: Francisco López de Gómara, Historia de la conquista de México

stops.name: Bahía de Santa Cruz, the sea that bears his name
stops.campa: Having sunk a fortune into failed expeditions up the Pacific coast under captains he cannot fully trust, Cortés sails in person at fifty to found a colony on the peninsula the pilots call California, landing at a bay he christens Santa Cruz for the day of arrival: today's La Paz. The colony starves within a year on a coast too dry to farm, and he abandons it, but the gulf he opened to Spanish charts keeps his name from that voyage onward: the Mar de Cortés, the one geographic feature on earth that will carry his name into ages that forget almost everything else he did.
suggested_refs: The Bahía de La Paz, Baja California Sur, christened Santa Cruz by Cortés in 1535

segments.name: The Cold Last Years and the Wandering Bones

stops.name: Off Algiers: the storm, the lost emeralds
stops.campa: Back in Spain and past fifty-five, denied the vast lawsuits he has filed to recover what he believes New Spain still owes him, Cortés volunteers for Charles V's expedition against Algiers, offered no command and treated as an aging curiosity by younger officers. An October storm wrecks over a hundred ships on the Barbary coast, drowning the campaign along with five matchless emeralds Cortés is said to have carried, carved into a bell, a rose, a fish, a horn, a little cup, gifts once meant for a queen, lost with the wreck of his last chance at glory in arms.
suggested_refs: The lost emeralds of Cortés, said drowned in the 1541 Algiers disaster
sources: Francisco López de Gómara, Historia de la conquista de México

stops.name: Valladolid, the carriage of the King
stops.campa: Following the itinerant court from town to town for years, unable to gain an audience, Cortés is said to have forced his way one day through the crowd pressing around the emperor's carriage and set his hand on its step. When Charles demanded to know who this man was who dared such familiarity, tradition, carried down through Voltaire and the historians after him, not found in the Spanish chronicles themselves, gives him the answer that has outlived every court record of the case: that he is the one who has given his king more provinces than his ancestors left him towns.
stops.quote: It is he who has given you more states than your ancestors left you cities.
stops.quote_source: Voltaire, Essai sur les moeurs et l'esprit des nations (1756); repeated by Prescott, History of the Conquest of Mexico (1843), not attested in Spanish chronicles of the period
suggested_refs: The itinerant court of Charles V, which Cortés followed unrewarded through his final Spanish years
sources: William H. Prescott, History of the Conquest of Mexico

stops.name: Castilleja de la Cuesta, the death
stops.campa: Broken in health, mired in decades of lawsuits over his fortune and his rights in New Spain, sixty-two years old, Cortés dies of pleurisy in the house of a friend at Castilleja de la Cuesta near Seville, still waiting on a passage back to the country he conquered and was never quite trusted to keep. His will names his legitimate son Martín heir to the marquisate, provides for his other children, among them Martín the younger, born of Doña Marina, and Leonor, born of Isabel Moctezuma, Moctezuma's own daughter, and asks that his bones, wherever they first rest, be carried at last to New Spain.
suggested_refs: The house at Castilleja de la Cuesta, Seville, where Cortés died in 1547
sources: Francisco López de Gómara, Historia de la conquista de México

stops.name: Mexico City, Hospital de Jesús: the wandering bones
stops.campa: The bones cross the ocean in 1566, rest in a Texcoco convent, move to a church in Mexico City, are hidden under floorboards during the anti-Spanish riots after Independence, lost track of for a century, and are finally identified in 1946 within a wall of the Hospital de Jesús: the hospital Cortés founded in 1524 on the very ground, tradition holds, where he and Moctezuma first stood face to face. Reinterred there in 1947 under a modest plaque, unmarked by any name outside, they rest today meters from that meeting: the one institution of his conquest that has never stopped doing the work he set it to.
suggested_refs: The Hospital de Jesús Nazareno, Mexico City, founded by Cortés in 1524, where his bones now rest
